title: What is Learning - 4
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton explains stickiness, the point at which repeated experience makes learning automatic, and then confronts an uncomfortable consequence: the brain does not care whether what it hardwires is good. Because brains are always on, children and adults learn whatever they repeatedly experience, including anger, shame, sexist attitudes or the habit of faking it. He illustrates with his own childhood fear of maths produced by his father's repeated anger, and with his early teaching, when his insecurities taught pupils lessons he never intended. He concludes that the quality and quantity of repeated experiences may be the biggest factor affecting learning and uses four classroom and home vignettes to ask what is being made sticky. The post amends his working definition of learning to include hardwiring.
points: Stickiness, meaning automatic and low-energy recall, is what separates a passing experience from learning.
Learning is not inherently good; brains hardwire whatever is repeated, so practice makes permanent for bad habits too.
Adults teach through the experiences they repeat, intended or not, as the author's maths anxiety and early teaching mistakes show.
Contradictions between what adults say and repeatedly do, such as caring assemblies delivered with shouting, teach the behaviour rather than the message.
quotes: Stickiness is a very important part of learning. Stickiness happens when the repeated experiences happen often enough to cause the learning to become automatic, recallable or redoable with very little energy wastage.
Without stickiness, we may have had some interesting experiences, but we haven’t learned anything. Stickiness and some aspects of memory are closely related.

When we think of learning as being good, we forget that the brain doesn’t really ‘care’ what it learns. On the whole, brains aren’t ‘interested’ in what is good. They ‘want’ to save energy by hardwiring what they repeatedly experience.

Unwittingly, he successfully helped me learn to associate maths with difficulty and unpleasantness. He did this through repeatedly communicating to me his mathematical frustration and anger at my inability to get the maths right.

The children and people I am with will learn best what I repeatedly enable them to experience. What I don’t repeatedly create for them will be much, much harder to learn. And, if what I repeatedly create for them isn’t ‘good’, then that’s still what they will learn.

Practice makes permanent. That's the good and bad news about learning in one three-word sentence. Learning is everything that has been hardwired, whether it is useful or not, high quality or not, good or not.

I have come to realise that the quality and quantity of the repeated experiences we create are probably the biggest factors that affect learning. This is true whether we are thinking of learning as academic, social, physical or emotional.
